text.en: The Sefer Chareidim, unlike other counts of the mitzvos, orders them by the limbs, and by opening with the heart rather than the head it signals that emunah, the first mitzvah of the heart, comes first of all.
Without emunah an act loses its identity as a mitzvah: a heretic who gives money gives charity, but not tzedakah, because tzedakah means giving because Hashem commanded it.
The 'apikorus' one must be ready to answer is not only the one standing opposite, but the one within a person's own heart.
Emunah in a Jew resembles the inborn knowledge of animals: just as a bee or beaver builds without being taught, a Jew believes by instinct, as an inheritance of the soul.
Creation was incomplete until Avraham Avinu, the first believer, came to perfect it, and the Jewish people's emunah traces back to him.
A kashya against an absolute truth is only a question, not a refutation, just as a helium balloon does not make a child doubt that things fall.

The Rav compares the ba'al teshuvah to the migrating bird: with no memory or instruments it returns to the very tree where it was born, and so the Jew's heart navigates him back to Hashem by an inherited sense.

Chiel of Beis El found a natural explanation for each son's death, a virus, a cold, a kidney disorder, because his ambition would not let him admit Yehoshua's curse; the Rav presents this as the model of rationalization.

Old people who return to observance once their desires are gone no longer need to rationalize, while those whose driving force is ga'avah grow even prouder in old age and cannot admit their life was folly.
Avraham Avinu had to be barren because he was a new species; had he been able to have children in the natural way, Yitzchak would simply have been a grandchild of Terach.
The Rav connects the hey added to Avraham's and Sarah's names with the power to have children, and brings that Bilhah's name has two heys, one for Rachel and one for herself.
From the kofer (tar) on Noach's ark and the kapores that covers the aron, the Rav explains that apikorsus is only a cover smeared over the emunah that remains inside.

The Megillah is read at night and again by day because the first reading only reveals at the end that every detail was part of the miracle; the second reading can then be said from the start with joy, praise and thanks.
The Megillah's episodes look like gossip columns a yeshiva bochur should not read, yet at the end they all lock together, which is the point: the miracle is hidden inside natural events.
History is to be studied with the depth one gives to a Tosafos; studied that way, it shows that the wars and fortunes of nations all revolve around the small Jewish people.
Hashem is in disguise in history; the Megillah teaches that He hides Himself and then appears through the miracle.
A forecaster only predicts what makes sense, but the Torah predicted what makes no sense, that a nation in exile would survive forever, and it came true.
Christianity took monotheism from the Jews but made religion easy by dropping Shabbos, Shemitah and the restrictions of Jewish family life, which, the Rav says, a non-Jew could not keep.
The seed and the tree can be seen both ways: every Yid was once in Avraham, and Avraham is now in every Yid, a 'gene' of emunah that nurtures him.
A kofer is one who covers up, as the word kofer means pitch that coats the ark; the emunah is underneath, flickering like a spark under sand.

First and last letters hold the whole word, as Rosh Hashanah holds the year and its last day holds it for teshuvah; Avner's name in the middle letters showed that only the temporary middle of a Yid can be lost, never his beginning or end.
The three matzos stand for the emunah of the three Avos and the four cups for the four Imahos, matching the three-headed and four-headed shin of the tefillin.
Dropping the final nun of 'amen' leaves 'em', mother: emunah, being feeling and instinct, is passed through the mother, which is why Jewishness alone among all traits follows her.
The Rav reads Chazal's linking of 'after your eyes' with heresy as cause and effect: a person does not become a heretic and then sin; he wants to sin and becomes a heretic to justify it.
Esav's claim that his wives cost him the brachos is the Rav's model of rationalization: he decides he himself is worthy and looks for something else to blame.
People avoid the Torah's account of creation not because of its content but because reading on leads to 'do not murder, do not steal', and one cannot drive through life with the brakes on.
Medical science itself assumes that every detail in the body has a purpose and searches for it, which is an admission of design.
Apparent conflicts between science and Torah resemble the Yemenite woman's kasha: they come from knowing Chumash without its meforshim, and are answered by learning more Torah, not less.

The Rav turns the skeptic's demand for proof around: the denier cannot be sure there is no Creator, and with real risks no one acts on a one-in-a-thousand doubt, so his position shows temptation, not logic.
The generation born in the desert, raised on bread from heaven, found wheat growing from the ground astonishing; we see the same wonder daily and are unmoved only because we are used to it.
Each organ is a wonder, yet none could exist without the others, and their interaction is itself a further wonder.
Hashem made food tasty and beautiful with many colors and distinct tastes, both so that a person will want to eat and stay healthy and as a display of chen.
If the body arose by itself, some parts should have no purpose; yet every organ once thought useless, like the appendix and tonsils, turned out to have one.
Denial of G-d is not a failure of belief but a deliberate covering up of belief, because a person who sees G-d cannot freely follow his desires; the boy compared it to driving with the brakes on.
Modern fears that progress and pollution will destroy the world are the same mistake as the Dor Haflagah, who built a tower to hold up the sky; Hashem who made the world maintains it.
Clotting that happens only on contact with air is itself the wonder: if blood clotted inside the veins it would cause thrombosis, strokes and heart attacks.
Water's exception to the rule of contraction in cold is a purposeful deviation: Hashem needs it for His world so that rivers freeze from the top and life survives below.
Just as ice has a pattern of behavior unique to it among the elements, Jews have a pattern of behavior different from the nations.
Yeshivos build their learning on resolving contradictions in the Rambam's halachos, yet leave his philosophy unlearned, and the Rav says there must be a reason for it.
Philosophy is like chess: a proof by a mind of IQ 200 falls before one of 300, so it can never establish a truth.
Understanding Hashem with the mind is not a matter of being smart enough; it is the wrong organ, like seeing a symphony with the eyes.
Weakness in emunah comes from aveiros, which insulate the neshamah from Hashem like the sheath on an electric wire.
The title Moreh Nevuchim shows the sefer was written for the lost, who are like a wet match that Torah cannot ignite until they first do teshuvah.
In Ein K'Elokeinu we say the answer, 'there is none like our G-d', before the question, 'who is like our G-d', because we do not trust ourselves with a kasha before the teretz.
The Rav reads the name 'teivel' for the earth as 'confusion', as in the eye blemish tevallul, so that the pasuk of the lightnings describes Hashem lighting up a world of confusion.
A flash of lightning lasts only a moment, yet it is enough to show a traveler which way the road goes; so too a brief revelation in the darkness gives direction.
According to the Rav, the absence of open wonders today is not because there are no tzaddikim, but because in hester panim they are not given permission to show them.
Through the Kotzker Rebbe's reply to the Apta Rav, the Rav teaches that believing is a higher level than seeing, so the generation of hiding has its own greatness.
The Rav describes our souls as sent down into this period of darkness on a mission, so that believing despite Hashem's disguise is the calling of this world.
The ten sedras of Devarim map the centuries of the sixth millennium, so the Rav reads Nitzavim-Vayelech, counted as one sedra, as the Torah's account of the century that began with Tav-Shin.
The hester panim of the end of the galus is doubled: not only does Hashem hide His face, the concealment itself is concealed, so people do not even see that He is hiding.
Moshe Rabbeinu wrote down the hester panim in advance as testimony, something the founders of other religions never dared to do, since only he knew his words would come true.

Preparing the refuah before the makah is what shows a surgeon is not a murderer, so for the Jewish people even the blow is part of the healing; Haman's decree itself was a yeshua that brought them to teshuvah.
Because a sedra is a 'program' of the world, galus and the geulah, though in one century, belong to two different orders and so need two sedras.
The teshuvah movement of today is a 'drizzle' of the full teshuvah of Mashiach's time, the beginning of Nitzavim's prophecy.

The variety among Jews is part of Klal Yisrael's beauty: like the twelve colored stones and flags of the shevatim, or apples on one tree that are never exactly alike, small differences coexist with an essential sameness.

The passuk's word order 'bechol she'arecha... lishvatecha' hints, according to a sefer the Rav cites, that each shevet has its own gate, like the gates of the shevatim at the end of Yechezkel and the twelve paths at the Yam Suf.

The ten makkos reproduced the ten maamaros of creation, so at Yetzias Mitzrayim the Jews saw Maaseh Bereishis and Hashem's control of nature; this is why the mitzvah of emunah is phrased as 'who took you out of Mitzrayim'.
The yetzer hara fights hardest just before Mashiach, like a flickering candle flame that flares up when it is about to go out.
Even saying 'would have' after a loss is already a blemish in emunah, since everything down to which end of a fallen straw points east is directed by Hashem.
The fiftieth gate differs from the other forty-nine in kind: they are midos, while it is daas, so in tumah it is not a bad trait but apikorsus itself.
In kedushah the right side and the giver lead, while in tumah the left and the receiver dominate; this is why the chesed of tumah is Canaani, a chesed that is subdued.
Just as emunah in kedushah is beyond reason, apikorsus in the fiftieth gate of tumah is also beyond reason: it defies logic, as in the claim that the ordered universe made itself.
Being tormented by doubts is itself a sign that one's soul stood at Sinai; one of the Erev Rav is not troubled by them but welcomes them.
Arguing with doubts only entangles a person further, like a fly struggling in a spider web, because the doubts are letzanus and do not respond to logic.
Unlike earlier ages, when people believed in idols, the present age is one of believing in nothing at all, which shows that the fiftieth gate of tumah now rules the world.
The shortening of the 400 years of Mitzrayim to 210 shows that even a decree written explicitly in the Torah need not be fulfilled in full, so the birth pains of Mashiach too can be reduced to fear.
In single hiding the child still knows his father is nearby and cries out to him; in hiding within hiding he does not even know there is anyone to call, which is the state before Mashiach.
The year is a miniature of all time: Nisan, from 'nes', a raised flag, is revealed miracle, while Adar, the end of the year, is like Esav born cloaked, with its miracles wrapped in nature.
The gossip about Vashti that a yeshiva boy rightly refused to hear became part of the Megillah, read with a brachah and indispensable to it; in the same way today's news is part of Hashem's plan.
Bitachon itself pierces the concealment: one who tells Hashem he relies on Him comes to see Hashem's care, breaking the hester panim.
The lack of great leaders whose word can be relied upon as the word of Hashem is itself foretold for the time before Mashiach, leaving the Jews to rely on Hashem alone.
The Rav reads the doubled 'haster astir' as two layers: in plain hiding one still knows the father is near and can call him; in the hiding within the hiding one does not even know he is there.
He sees the year as a miniature of all time: Nisan, from 'nes', a banner raised high, is open miracles, while Adar at its end is the hidden miracles of the end of days.

The news story about Vashti that pious bochurim would have shut out of the beis medrash became part of the Megillah, so that one who skips it has not fulfilled the mitzvah; so too today's news is part of a Megillah being written.
The Rav explains that bitachon itself breaks through the hester panim: the one who tells Hashem he relies on Him comes to see Hashem's care.
Yishmael is harder than Rome or Bavel because, as a 'pere adam' who stays wild whatever his profession, he cannot be reasoned with or moved by mercy.
The Rav reads the physical waves of the sea as the lower waters' yearning to rise to the King, so that a law of physics reflects a law of creation.
Nisuch hamayim gave the lower waters their way to serve Hashem, which is why they began weeping again when the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed.
Following the Yismach Moshe, the exiles by the rivers of Babylon wept 'also' because they wept together with the weeping waters; both were separated from closeness to Hashem.
The passuk that Hashem praises the rising waves teaches that effort is praised even where it cannot succeed; a Jew's effort, unlike the waves', does succeed.
The pauses in music and the blank spaces of the shira in the Sefer Torah show that a person's empty periods are themselves part of his song, not interruptions of it.
Every creature sings by being what it is, but man alone chooses whether to sing along; the tzaddik, the neshama of the last verse of Tehillim, conducts the whole orchestra of creation.
Preparing on Friday for Shabbos while gathering no man for tomorrow mirrors life: one should worry about the 'tomorrow' of Olam Haba and store up mitzvos, not about tomorrow in this world.

The Israelites' doubt at Masa uMeriva is the snake's original venom: following the Megaleh Amukos, the letters of 'hayesh' and 'ayin' make up 'hishiani', the word Chava used for the snake's enticement.
The kasha eaten on Shabbos Shira is a lesson in emunah: learn to 'swallow a kasha', even a black one, and remain a believing Jew.
If the Jewish tree yields sour fruit, perhaps the fault is in the soil and not the tree; replanted in the Beis HaMikdash, as the shira ends, it will yield golden fruit.
The missing vav in Eliezer's retelling marks the moment his hidden interest surfaced: only once Rivka was certain to marry Yitzchak could he see that 'perhaps' had meant 'to me'.
Theories about how the world works are like guessing at a watch's mechanism while the watchmaker's own book lies in the library: the Creator wrote the Chumash.
In Lashon HaKodesh a verb ending in nun loses it as a noun, so aman, to believe, becomes em, mother, showing that emunah comes from the mother.
Trying to grasp G-d with the mind is like trying to hear a painting: the failure is not weakness of the organ but using the wrong sense altogether.
Sins act like insulation on a live wire, cutting the mind off from the neshamah's contact with G-d; a tzaddik still feels some of the current, to the degree of his righteousness.
Ein Keloheinu is said before Mi Keloheinu so that the answer comes before the question, since even a moment of entertaining the question without the answer is a departure from emunah.

On Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol, the Kodesh HaKodashim of souls, enters the Kodesh HaKodashim of space on the Kodesh HaKodashim of time, and the atonement comes from the strength each dimension draws from contact with the others.
Our generation is the toenail of the soul of Klal Yisrael, but Jews who keep Torah and mitzvos are the living part of the nail that still hurts if cut away.
Adar is named for 'aderes', a cloak: the month of concealment, the opposite of Nisan, though Hashem is as present in it as in Nisan.
The greater the hester panim, the greater the miracle that Klal Yisrael survives at all.

HaMelech, Haman and 'kes Kah' all equal 95, so Haman's presence is what turns Hashem's revealed Name into the veiled 'HaMelech'; 'macho emcheh' equals 107, the value of the Throne and Name made whole.
The Megillah is a training in reading between the lines; once mastered, one can read the newspaper and see Hashem's name in it.
Because the world was created with loshon hakodesh, its words explain their own concepts: Atzilus from 'etzel', near Hashem, and 'olam' from 'ne'elam', concealed.
Menucha is not rest but gratification, like a worker whose exhausting Sunday soccer game is his menucha; Shabbos menucha is the feeling of having reached one's goal and lacking nothing.
'L'hodos' means both to thank and to agree, as in 'the Chachamim agree with Rabbi Meir': in the future we will agree that whatever Hashem did was right.
'Boker' is related to 'bikur', examining: in the light one can inspect and understand, while 'layla' is related to 'yelala', wailing, the time when only emunah helps.
'Asor' comes from 'ashirus', rich and gratifying tunes, and 'navel' means wretched tunes; 'higayon b'chinor' means to think into the tune Hashem is playing, whichever it is.
The joy of 'simachtani' does not depend on the tune: it comes from knowing that Hashem's attention is focused on me, whether He grants happiness or surgical pain.
Fruit trees do not grow tall because they put their strength into fruit, while tall trees give no fruit; the tzaddik will have both, like the palm and the cedar together.
The vav missing in the written 'avlasa' is the vav of connection: today we do not see how events connect, but in the future the vav will be read and all of history will fit together.
The Rav explains that in the future Midas haDin itself will dictate chesed: the Jewish people will be on such a level that they will be comfortable being judged strictly.
Following the Hafla'ah, the date palm stays short because it puts its strength into fruit; so a tzaddik who spends himself on talmidim is promised that he will still grow tall like the cedar.
Hashem chose Avraham Avinu over Chanoch, even though Chanoch rose to the level of a malach, because Avraham lowered himself to reach and draw close other people.
Yaakov wanted to leave the womb despite having a malach as his rebbe, because sharing a classroom with Esav was worse than losing such a rebbe; friends count for more than the rebbe.
Avraham had Yishmael and Yitzchak had Esav first, because each had to discharge the bad side of his attribute, bad chesed and bad din, before giving rise to holy offspring.
The European habit of putting the left first, buttoning left over right, 'ladies first', and writing from the left, reflects Esav's attribute of din, female before male.

In Tammuz the Shem Havaya appears backwards and at the ends of the words of 'zeh einenu shoveh li', the harshest din; 'lehagid ki yashar Hashem' teaches that even this will be revealed as the Shem straight, chesed.
Klal Yisrael's long waiting in galus is itself a tikkun for Adam HaRishon, whose sin was that he did not wait: had he waited until Shabbos he could have made kiddush on the wine of the tree.
The past tense Hashem Malach is the song of the days of Mashiach: only in hindsight will it be clear that Hashem reigned throughout the galus, when all the questions find their answers.

Ge'us lavesh does not mean Hashem is proud; it describes how it appears to one without emunah, as though Hashem has retired from caring for the low world, and the double lavesh means even the hiding is hidden.
Hashem needed oz, courage, to hide Himself in galus, like a surgeon father operating on his own child, who feels the child's pain more than any other doctor.

The world is called Tevel because to the non-believer it is a blurred mixture, like a vision with astigmatism, seen only in brief flashes of lightning; the pasuk promises that this very Tevel will not slip.
The word me'olam relates to concealment: Hashem is present in a hidden way and governs the world peeking out from the cracks, and because He is hidden the nations rise up like rivers.

The rivers are individual kingdoms and the breakers of the sea are empires that rule many countries, and the same nations that now raise their voice against Klal Yisrael will one day raise it to lament their own downfall.
Emunah is a hereditary instinct in a Jew, just as a beaver isolated from birth still builds a dam and a spider spins its mother's web; Avraham Avinu introduced a new species into creation.
A Jew who denies Hashem is not lacking emunah but has a sick emunah, like a man who ate sawdust and lost his hunger; aveiros and forbidden food clog the heart.
Unlike faiths founded on one charismatic individual, the Torah rests on an event experienced by millions at once, which can no more be faked than the existence of George Washington or Julius Caesar.
Rashi's question is answered by the Rambam's principle: milah is kept only because Moshe Rabbeinu told it, so the first mitzvah received through Moshe, HaChodesh hazeh lachem, is truly the first.
The nation's first mitzvah is by its very character renewal: a new moon out of a dark sky, a new nation out of dark Mitzrayim, and so the nation carries the message that one can always renew oneself.
Pesach is the only moed with kares because its essence is kesher, a new bond with Hashem; the one who misses it is cut off.
The renewal of nature in Nisan is an impact of the nation's renewal in that month, which enters even into physical nature.
Adar, from 'aderes', a cloak, is the month furthest from Nisan: Nisan's miracles are revealed, Adar's are wrapped in nature, a nes twelve levels removed from an open nes.
For a child raised in the desert on the mann, bread rising from the ground would be the wonder; what we call nature is a miracle we are simply used to.
The news of the day is a Megillah being written now: events like Russia's collapse just before the Gulf War are pieces of one plan to protect the Jews.
Gossip from the king's court that a yeshiva boy rightly refuses to hear was, in Shushan, the very unfolding of the nes without which the Jews would not exist today.
Just as 'HaMelech' in the Megillah alludes to Hashem, a believer reading about the president in the newspaper understands that the real ruler is Hashem, and the leaders are marionettes.
Purim masks teach that the whole world is a masked world, and under the mask Hashem directs nations, families and every small happening.
Read event by event, the Megillah contains nothing a newspaper could not report; its miracle lies only in how the natural events fit together.
Natural growth of wheat is as great a miracle as the manna; the children born in the desert, used to bread from heaven, saw bread from the ground as the wonder.
The months descend from Nisan, named for open miracles, to Adar, whose name means a cloak, so Adar's miracles are the cloaked ones.
The Rav calls the Megillah's hidden miracles 'even bigger' than the supernatural miracles of the Exodus.
Purim's costumes become a lesson: the world's kings and rulers are only dressed in the 'aderes' of Adar, while Hashem controls them from behind.

The Rav argues that the fulfillment of Moshe's prophecies is a proof the nations' scriptures cannot offer, since they avoided predictions, and the one they made, that Jews would never return, has failed.
He describes the present as late afternoon of the world's Erev Shabbos: after chatzos of the sixth day, when one is already going to the mikveh and preparing the candles.
Hester within hester is a child who not only cannot see his hidden father but does not even know a father is there; this, says the Rav, is the state of those who lost their emunah in the Holocaust.

The difference between a blow followed by a cure and a cure prepared before the blow is the difference between a stabbing and surgery: a surgeon who prepared the bandages beforehand shows the cutting itself is for healing.
Nitzavim and Vayelech are one sedra in count, matching one century, yet two sedras in theme, because galus and geulah are separate; in the geulah no pain of galus will remain.

Creation is pictured as baking challah for Shabbos: Adam was the first 'challah of the world' and failed, the world after Noach failed again, and only the third, Avraham, rose and produced a people fit for the day that is entirely Shabbos.

A sin a person stumbles into should prompt the further question 'where is my emunah?', because with clear knowledge that Hashem is watching, as one would behave before a great tzaddik, the sin could not have happened.
Emunah outranks the other mitzvos because it was received directly from Hashem at Sinai in the first two commandments, while the rest came through Moshe Rabbeinu.

Talk that treats the election of a president as deciding the world's course holds a 'piece of apikorsus', since the president cannot dip his finger in cold water without Hashem's power and permission.

The suffering in Egypt was measure for measure: the souls of the generation of the dispersion, who built with bricks and mortar, were punished with bricks and mortar, and those of the flood generation were thrown into the river.

The Akeidah's test was the kushya, not the sacrifice: idol worshippers burned their own children, but a non-Jew abandons his god when he has a question, whereas Avraham, like a Jew covering his eyes at Shema, refused to look at the kushya.

The Rav argues from the form of the verse that the Ramban appears right: a mitzvah means a command, yet 'Anochi Hashem' is written as a statement, Hashem presenting Himself, not as an order to believe.
Instinctive knowledge in animals, which no one taught them and which belongs to their very being, serves as the model for the emunah a Jew is born with.
Avraham's novelty as a 'new creation' was not physical, since he and his children see like other people, but a knowledge of Hashem that the nations do not have.
The small heh of 'behibaram' is read as 'b'Avraham': the world was completed when Avraham received the heh, the letter of birth, at his bris.
Avraham was created barren so that his line from Terach would be cut, and the new power of birth given with the heh began a new people; this is why Yitzchak has no connection to Terach.
The Rav reads 'vehe'emin' as written without a yud, the letter of chochmah, to show that Avraham's emunah was natural and not built on intellect.
The alef-beis order of the chapters of praise is itself a statement: David has not finished Hashem's praises, he stops only because the letters are finished.
The exact share of oxygen in the air is a wonder of balance in both directions: less would choke every creature, and more would turn one fire into the burning of the whole world.
The renewal of the body every seven years gives a way to understand a little of gilgul, a soul coming down again in another body.
That the brain cells alone are not renewed is itself the wonder that allows memory: new cells would not hold what was engraved in the old ones, like a calculator that loses its numbers.
A gentile's readiness to die for his country is the product of daily drilling from childhood, while the Jew's readiness to die for his emunah comes from emunah in the heart, inherited from the Avos.

Rashi's question why the Torah did not begin with 'Hachodesh' is tied to the foundation of emunah: Hachodesh was the first mitzvah Moshe taught on the strength of the appointment the people heard at Sinai.
Even mitzvos with a tradition from Avraham, like milah, or from Yaakov, like gid hanasheh, are binding not because of that individual but because Moshe was commanded at Sinai to teach them.
The halachic rule that one wrong letter invalidates a Sefer Torah, together with the mitzvah for every Jew to write one, kept every Sefer Torah an exact copy for thousands of years.

Differences in halachah between tribes reflect middas chesed and middas din, both from Hashem; this is why each tribe needed its own judges, and why Beis Hillel tends to leniency and Beis Shammai to stringency.
The claim of other faiths that Hashem changed His mind comes not from reason but from their inability to accept that the Jews are the chosen people.
Today's hatred of the Jews cannot be explained by religious difference, since the nations themselves no longer keep their faith; its secret is in Vayeshev: jealousy of the beloved son.

The Rav argues that seeking Hashem with the intellect is a category error, like claiming to listen to a painting or to see a symphony; Hashem is perceived through a different faculty, akin to nevuah and ruach hakodesh, which Klal Yisroel as a whole still has.
The proof from Sinai, as the Rav reads the Yismach Moshe, lies in transmission: a fabricated event would be exposed at once, since children would find that neither they nor their friends had seen it.

The Rambam could engage in inquiry without danger because he felt Hashem so tangibly that denial never occurred to him even while posing the questions; even his yiras shamayim in a state of katnus was too much for the Yismach Moshe.
In Ein Kelokeinu the declaration 'there is none like our G-d' comes before the question 'who is like our G-d', teaching that a Jew begins with the answer of emunah and only then may ask.

The Rav applies the image of Adam haRishon's body twice: within each generation, where the head, heart and hands are the Torah scholars, the masters of tefillah and the givers of tzedakah; and across all history, where the desert generation is the head and ours the heel.
The heel's lack of sensation explains why emunah feels weak today: like a tooth pulled after a numbing injection, the emunah is present but not felt.
Because the people of the last generation are so small, their avodah is more precious to Hashem, just as a king delights more in a parrot's few words than in the wisdom of his ministers.
Because emunah belongs to the heart, and the heart and mind are life itself, a person who lacks emunah does not merely lack one limb at techiyas hameisim but cannot rise at all.
Yaakov, fleeing danger, asked only for bread and a garment because he meant the soul's needs in the next world: Torah as its food and mitzvos as its garments.
Just as clothing costs more than food, mitzvos cost more than Torah: anyone can learn, but a mezuzah or tefillin costs money.
Chavakuk basing all the mitzvos on emunah does not free anyone from the others; it means concentrating on one mitzvah through which all the others are kept.
Emunah is like a building's basement: no one counts it as a room, yet it holds the furnace and boiler that make the whole building livable.
Love of Hashem can be commanded, unlike loving a food, because every Jew already loves Hashem inwardly; the mitzvah is to bring it out into the open.
The Rav uses the inborn knowledge of animals, such as a spider that never saw its mother yet weaves her exact web, as a model for how emunah can be inherited by a Jew.
The mitzvah of 'Anochi Hashem' is phrased as a fact because the Jew already believes; the command within it is not to spoil what he was born with.
Weak emunah is not an absence but an illness: like a man who ruined his appetite with a bad breakfast, the desire is there and only needs treatment.
Forbidden food and arayos are the spiritual cholesterol of the soul, clogging the heart of emunah as cholesterol blocks the arteries.
As the first tree contained every tree that would grow from its seeds, every Jew was once actually part of Avraham, and Yaakov held within him Avraham and Yitzchak.
Although a trait usually thins out over generations, it grows stronger when both partners carry it; since Klal Yisrael all descends from Avraham, Jews are almost entirely Avraham.
Chazal locate heresy in the heart rather than the mind: the verse warns against straying 'after your hearts', and the heart is the seat of desires, so kefirah is born of wanting, not of thinking.
Chiel of Beis El, burying son after son as Yehoshua's curse came true and still building, is the Navi's picture of denial: a person can watch the truth happen before his eyes and refuse to admit it.

The evolving, constantly revised theories of creation are themselves a sign of rationalization: having rejected the Chumash's account for reasons of the heart, the apikores must keep rewriting his own.
The Rav compares rejecting the Torah to the nations who refused it at Sinai: they too rejected it because a particular commandment opposed their nature, not because it made no sense.

The two driving forces of the soul, taivah and gaavah, explain who returns at the end of life: when desire fades the excuse is gone and people do teshuvah, but gaavah does not leave with age, and admitting a life lived in error would wound the ego.

Philosophy is not a Jewish article: no Gemara or Midrash anywhere tries to establish the foundations of emunah through logical arguments, and the Rav takes this absence itself as a sign that it is a foreign import.
Trying to grasp Hashem with the intellect is like trying to hear a picture: even hearing a million times sharper would not help, because it is the wrong faculty altogether, not a weak one.
The sudden flash that makes a whole sugya clear to a simple, upright Jew is a small appearance of the ruach hakodesh that every Jew has through his neshamah.
Aveiros act like the insulation on an electric wire: the current of the neshamah is still there, but the person has no contact with it.

One need not survey the whole creation to see the Creator; a person's own body, with its self-adjusting and self-repairing systems, is enough, which is the meaning the Rav gives to 'from my flesh I see G-d'.
The Rav compares the world to the body: just as no system of the body can exist without the others, no part of nature, from plants to planets, can exist without the rest.
Denying a Creator is not an intellectual conclusion but a rationalization: people make themselves blind because recognizing the Ribono shel Olam would put the brakes on their desires.
The brain cells that never get replaced are what make memory possible, so that a person still remembers the aleph-beis he learned as a small child.
Water behaves like every other substance until it nears freezing, and only then reverses, precisely so that ice floats and life in rivers survives the winter.

The Rav traces the Maharsham's well-known leniency in psak to the instruction he received from Reb Ayzikl of Zidichov after being saved, that making things hard for Jews is no skill and one must make things easy.

In the story, the defense that saves the Maharsham is that in a bitter exile with so much hiding of Hashem's face, a young man sitting and learning Torah is very precious above, even if not purely for Heaven's sake.
The Rav reads the Kotzker Rebbe's reply as a deep point: though he is sure the Kotzker also saw the ushpizin, he chose to say that he believes, because believing is greater than seeing.

The Rav presents the concentration of Kohanim and Levi'im among halachic authorities, from the Shulchan Aruch's commentators to the roshei yeshiva of his own beis medrash, as a visible, present-day proof of the truth of Moshe Rabbeinu's blessing.
The Rav contrasts the Chassidic Rebbes, among whom one does not find this pattern of Kohanim and Levi'im, but rather descent from the royal house of David.

The Rav reads the Yaavetz as showing empirically that philosophical proofs of faith fail under trial: those who had proven Hashem's truth by logic converted, while those without such proofs went into exile for their faith.
Because the whole of Jewish faith rests on Yetzias Mitzrayim and Matan Torah as transmitted to one's children, the Rav says it is especially important to learn the sedros now being read.

Even differences of girsa that remain between Rashi and Tosafos are, in the Rav's view, both true, like a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, since Hashem allowed both readings to stand among the gedolim who learned them.
The Rav points out that Shaarei Teshuvah, one of the most important mussar works, came about as a direct result of Rabbeinu Yonah's teshuvah over his part in the burning of the Rambam's works.

The Rav explains Chavakuk's founding all mitzvos on emunah not as a release from the other mitzvos but as a response to shrinking generations, who can no longer concentrate on everything and must make one mitzvah the foundation.
The Megillah is read a second time because only after reaching its end does one understand how each detail at its beginning was part of the miracle; the second reading is read with that knowledge.
The Rav applies the Megillah model to all of Jewish history from Yetzias Mitzrayim until today: every part of it is a part of the miracle.
The hatred of the nations toward the Jews comes from envy, because they see that the Jew is better, as with Yosef's brothers; and despite that hatred they cannot swallow the Jews up.

Yitzchak and Yishmael were brothers, yet Yishmael's descendants number over three hundred million while the Jews number about fifteen million; this smallness was itself foretold, and the small people is the one that endures.
The Septuagint, translated by the elders long before the churban, preserves the Torah's text from that time, so the claim that passages were written in later cannot stand.

The idolatry in Tanach is no more a rejection of the Torah than the trials of the internet are for observant Jews today: both are a powerful yetzer hara in which people stumble while still keeping the Torah.
The present wave of baalei teshuvah is the drizzle that, as the Gemara describes, signals the coming downpour: the storm of teshuvah when Mashiach comes.
The proof lies not in any single prophecy but in their combination: each wonder contradicts the others and reason, like fact A contradicting fact B, so no historian could have extrapolated them.
Hatred of the Jews follows the natural dislike of the unlike: the greater the difference, the greater the hatred, and the separation between Israel and the nations is the greatest of all.
The German Jews' mistake was to think assimilation would end the hatred; instead it grew, and Hitler counted as Jews even those whose families had converted three generations earlier.
Unlike individual suicide bombers, whole Jewish communities chose death rather than conversion, a mesiras nefesh no other nation has shown.

Since the Torah is the blueprint of the world, the first time a thing appears in it defines it; the first 'ezer', Chava, was given to Adam only after all his efforts failed and he slept, so help by its nature comes without human action, an exercise in bitul.

The Gemara's laws of sukkah focus on sleeping rather than eating, because sleep is the essence of the sukkah: only one who feels secure can sleep, and the sukkah is a flimsy hut under Hashem's protection.
Nature is itself a Torah: a bird flying fulfills a command of the Torah just as a Jew putting on tefillin does, the only difference being that man has free choice.

Because nature is written in the Torah, a miracle that changes nature changes the Torah, which is why the Gemara criticizes the man for whom nature was changed and why tzaddikim avoided making miracles.

Creation keeps its Torah only when man keeps his: in the generation of the flood even the animals strayed from their kinds, while in the generation of the desert nature flourished so that one cluster of grapes needed eight men.

Bereishis is a history of three strikes against mankind, Adam, the flood and the dispersion, after which the keys of creation passed to Avraham, and even then the nations were given a last chance at Sinai.

The nations' claim to Eretz Yisrael, unlike any other land taken by conquest, comes from its being the center and root of creation, which even its name, the Mediterranean, 'middle of the land', reflects.
The Rav reads the Midrash that even a poor man may not eat on Pesach night until he reclines as teaching the essence of the Exodus: a Jew must have Someone to lean on, the Ribono shel Olam.
Playing on the custom of eating kasha on Shabbos Shirah, the Rav says the parsha of shirah and emunah teaches a Jew to swallow a kushya and remain a Jew.
The word mazal means a flow or channel: each person has a particular channel through which his flow of blessing comes down.
Before birth every soul agrees to the mazal it is given, since it knows that this is what its tikkun requires; only once clothed in the body does it no longer see what is good for it.
The drive, energy and aggressiveness of successful businessmen are not the cause of their wealth but part of the mazal of wealth they were created with, so dishonesty adds nothing.
The career choices of a yeshiva bachur carry a 'casualty rate' for the soul just as a war carries one for the body, and people fear the second far more only for lack of emunah.
The Jewish tree, like a citrus tree, cannot grow in foreign soil; the Rav sees 'tevi'emo vetita'emo' in this parsha as a prayer that Hashem transplant the Jews to where they truly belong.

The Rav reads the Midrash that even a poor man must recline, learned from 'vayasev', as saying that the forty years in the desert were a forty-year haseivah: the manna taught the Jews to lean on Hashem, and in that leaning rich and poor are equal.
Since every mitzvah contains Hashem's Name, the Arizal's practice of keeping the afikoman under the haseivah cushion means one is literally leaning on the Ribono shel Olam.
Amalek equals 'safek' (doubt) in gematria, so Moshe's hands that were 'emunah' were the direct answer to Amalek.

The desert generation is the youth of Klal Yisrael, and as a young man's years of learning set a habit for life, the forty years of learning set the habit of Torah for all later generations; this is the lesson of the long way around.

Serach bas Asher, who brought Yaakov the good news that Yosef lives, was clothed with the full aspect of Eliyahu; therefore she lives forever, counts as two in the seventy souls, and knew the secret of the redemption.

Because the redemption from Egypt was incomplete, the ox of the Merkavah, which is Yosef, had not yet been changed to a keruv; so Moshe called 'come up, ox' and the women sang their own feminine song, the song Perek Shirah gives the ox.

Beshalach's haftarah is Devorah's song, ending in forty years of quiet, while Shvi'i shel Pesach reads Dovid's song, ending in everlasting salvation, because Beshalach is only the reading of the Exodus while Shvi'i shel Pesach is its time.
Humor eases suffering precisely because it denies reality, carrying a person into a world of fantasy where the trouble does not exist; the same power is what makes it destructive.
Hashem's 'mockery' of Egypt was measure for measure: Pharaoh had resisted the plagues by joking about them, so Hashem turned Egypt into a joke.
Amalek's jump into the boiling bath was itself a joke: everyone laughed, the awe of Israel became humor, and so other nations lost their fear of attacking them.
Because Adar's organ is the spleen, the organ of laughter, the month of Amalek's defeat is when laughter is turned back against avodah zarah and the wicked.
A joke about the rebbe needs no argument at all, yet it cuts the rope of mesorah that stretches from rebbe to talmid back to Moshe at Sinai.
Against emes no logic can prevail; only the falsehood and fantasy of a joke can push it away, which is why the final war against Hashem is fought with jokes and Hashem answers with laughter.
Amalek attacked right after the Jews asked whether Hashem is among them: a lapse in emunah is what opened the door to Amalek, whose essence is casting doubt.
Even a prayer for something trivial, like winning color war, is an act of emunah, because it shows the belief that Hashem can help.
Avraham's trial at the Akeidah was not the willingness to give his son, which he already had, but going on with joy in the face of an apparent contradiction to Hashem's promise.
Closing the eyes at Shema expresses accepting Hashem's kingship blindly, without seeing or understanding, with readiness for mesirus nefesh.
History has months like the year: Nisan is the time of open miracles, while our era is history's Adar, the hidden last month before the end.
The 'sefer' in Daniel in which those to be saved are written is the 'sefer zikaron' of Malachi, which records those who hold on to emunah.

The Rav reads 'Rosh' Hashanah like the first letter of a word, which already holds the whole word in potential: the whole year is contained in Rosh Hashanah, and in the same way Haazinu contains the whole Torah.
Haazinu itself answers the question of why the Jews of Europe did not resist: one could chase a thousand only because Hashem had handed them over, and Haazinu foretold it.
Jews rejoice in the Day of Judgment because they want to be judged by Hashem Himself, like a child who runs to his mother even knowing she may slap him.
What comes from Hashem can be bitter but never bad, like a bitter wine that is in fact excellent, as only a connoisseur knows.
The hundred sounds of the shofar correspond to the ten utterances of creation, each including ten, so that hearing the shofar is like standing at the root of the year's whole course.

Malchiyos opens with Aleinu because Yehoshua said it when he broke through the walls of Yericho: accepting Hashem's kingship means breaking the wall around one's own heart to reach the point of yechidah.
Rebbi's suffering for the calf was not a punishment that Yom Kippur could atone for, but a reality: Hashem's mercy toward a person follows that person's own mercy.
The lowest generation is like the heels: the lowest part of the body, yet the whole body stands on them, so all the generations stand on ours and Moshiach comes specifically to it.
The generation that is the foundation of all generations is tested in emunah, the foundation of all mitzvos.
The Satan obstructs exactly the mitzvah a generation was created to fulfil: tzitzis in the Divrei Chaim's time, emunah in ours.
Fighting doubts is like a fly in a spider's web: the more it struggles to tear itself free, the more it is stuck, so doubts must be dismissed rather than debated.
Just as the geulah of Klal Yisroel has a fixed time but can be hastened by merit, each Jew has a private geulah from his trials that prayer and mesiras nefesh can bring sooner.
Amalek is numerically equal to 'safek' (doubt), so struggling against doubts in emunah is itself the mitzvah of the war against Amalek.
Torah is the mind and tefillah the heart, the two chief organs; one without the other is not enough.

Sefer Shemos is read precisely in the dark weeks of Teves because it belongs to a level above time and above the rule of the forces of darkness; a Jew whose mind is in the parshiyos of geulah is lifted out of the darkness, since a person is where his thoughts are.

Read as a preview of history, Bereishis reaches the days of Moshiach right where Yaakov seeks to live in peace, and the sale of Yosef breaks off the picture: this world is not equipped to display the joy of the days of Moshiach.

'Shamos' in 'asher sam shamos ba'aretz' is not plain destruction but a destruction that arouses wonder, related to shamayim, what is beyond our senses; and 'al tikri shamos ela shemos' teaches that each such wonder is a mission.
Pharaoh first gave the midwives Egyptian names, Shifrah and Puah, so that the power of evil in those names would draw them into his trap before he ordered them to kill.

Rashi identifies Dasan and Aviram by the small sin of leaving over the manna because it reveals the root of all their later rebellion: a lack of bitachon, which led them to worry about a livelihood, seek careers among the Egyptians and learn chutzpah.

The Torah inserts 'veYosef haya veMitzrayim' into the book of geulah to distinguish Yosef, who was forced into the high places of Egypt and therefore protected, from Dasan and Aviram, who chose to go there.
Leitzanus is not mere lightheadedness: it is the power to deny what one's own mind recognizes, which makes it the exact counterpart of emunah, the power to believe beyond what the mind sees.
Pharaoh could withstand plague after plague, though he clearly saw the hand of Hashem, only because a good joke gave him and his people relief and courage to deny what they saw.

The Rambam's ruling that Moshiach need not show signs elevates him: Eliyahu needed fire from heaven, while Avraham, and Moshiach after him, draw the world by the truth of their word alone; needing a sign would be a disgrace for Moshiach.

Esav was not an unbeliever: he grew up seeing angels and ruach hakodesh in Yitzchak's home, and his weeping over the brachos shows he believed; his kefirah was the kefirah of leitzanus, mocking away what he knew.

The principle of the se'ir la'azazel, giving the sitra achra a measured portion only as the Torah directs, explains the seudah at a siyum, shadchan money, and Yaakov's 'mirmah', which he did only by Rivka's prophecy.
Since Yaakov had already received the blessing of the existing world, Esav had to be given something that did not yet exist, Italia shel Yavan, formed later in the sea.
Mockery is the exact opposite of emunah: emunah holds on even without understanding, while mockery throws off even what is understood, not by argument but with a laugh.
The 'klipah' of the Plishtim is mockery: they could not answer Avraham's greatness, so they stopped up his wells by laughing at it.
The hard labor of Mitzrayim was itself a stopping of the wells: it left a Jew no time to think.
Each modern plan to end antisemitism, by assimilating in Germany or by building a nation, ended by making it worse, showing that fleeing the Ribono shel Olam does not work.
Through Rebbe Reb Bunim's vort on 'like a lost sheep', the Rav explains why the nations excuse in every other people what they condemn in the Jews.
The Ba'al Shem Tov was a neshamah not in keeping with his generation, one that could have lived in the time of the nevi'im, just as the Gra, though centuries later, could stand with the Rishonim.
Dovid HaMelech became the fourth leg of the Divine chariot in the very moment he accepted Shimi's curse, without a night of thought, as decreed by Hashem.
Klal Yisrael across history is one body: the dor hamidbar is the head, later eras lower down, and our generation the heel, the lowest part, which is redeemed through emunah.
The new devices of our time are a new creation of the yetzer hara, who fights emunah so hard because he knows that emunah brings the redemption and his own slaughter.

'Vayar es hamakom merachok' means that at the akeidah Avraham was put into small mind and felt Hashem far away, and in that state of a simple Jew of ikvesa dimeshicha he passed the test of our generation.
Hashem's double 'Avraham, Avraham' after the akeidah expresses His love for the last generation, which passes the same test.
A nisayon comes from the word nes, a raised banner: each test lifted Avraham to a higher level.
Trying to grasp Hashem with the intellect is like trying to hear a painting or see a symphony: each faculty has its own object, and the intellect is not the one for Hashem.

The neshamah is not bound by space and time; a person cannot see beyond the wall or into tomorrow only because sin insulates him from his own neshamah, while tzaddikim who purify the body 'crystal clear' have ruach hakodesh.
The minhag of Klal Yisroel serves as a proof in halachah because Klal Yisroel as a collective has ruach hakodesh even today.

Unlike other faiths built on one man's word, Jewish emunah rests on an event an entire nation witnessed; a fabricated claim of national revelation would have been exposed at once, as Holocaust denial is absurd.
Like a falling stone that gathers speed, the spiritual decline between generations accelerates, so the gap between our generation and the one before it is greater than between Yehoshua and Moshe.
'Dor l'dor yeshabach ma'asecha' means that what Hashem's middas hadin did in one generation is understood in a later one, when it is revealed retroactively as part of Klal Yisroel's tikkun.
'B'chen' in Birkas Hamazon: Hashem could have sustained man with a plain nutrient fuel, like a car, but chose to feed him with beauty, taste and variety.
The Rav reads the extra vav of 'u'gedulascha' as a connection: Dovid HaMelech sees the bond between every single thing and Hashem, and tells of it calmly, as a narrative, not as a surprise.
Buying a bottle of milk so as to have strength to daven or to learn with a bochur makes a great impression in Heaven, while a famous lecture reported in the newspapers makes none.
The Rav notes that a wind requires atmospheric changes over miles; to cool one worm, Hashem changed the whole region.
The souls of a terrible generation are like a kugel made of Shabbos leftovers: Hashem gathers damaged souls of many generations into one and mixes them into something good.

A life with a bad wife or in poverty, which Chazal count as no life, lets a soul that has used up its three chances come down again, since the accuser cannot claim it has really returned to the world.
'The nega did not turn its ayin' means the letter ayin did not move: a nega that is not turned around stays a nega instead of becoming oneg.
Causing others to act is greater than acting: tzaddikim are called Hashem's 'handiwork' because they cause Hashem to act, as a tzaddik decrees and Hashem fulfills.

The Rav reads 'sivro' (his hope) as 'shivro' (his breaking): since a person must be broken in any case, the sign of true hope in Hashem is that he breaks himself for Hashem, in toil over Torah and avodas Hashem.
A person's lifetime is described as a process of being broken, 'teitzei rucho yashuv l'admaso', so his suffering is not wasted if he directs it into his avodah.
The Rav compares seeing Hashem behind a helper to looking through an X-ray: among all who come to help, one sees Hashem Himself coming to help.

'Tziyon' is not only a place: when there is no Beis HaMikdash, the source of bitachon is found in Tziyon of the soul, the tzaddik and talmid chacham, and in Tziyon of time, Shabbos and other holy times; this is 'Elokayich Tziyon l'dor vador'.
Bringing a hidden spark of holiness out before its time is like taking the geulah by force: Hashem brings it out through means such as bitul b'rov, but a person may not do it himself.

The Rav explains that Dovid HaMelech, having finished Tehillim with Ashrei, could not hold back his appetite for praise and added 'Hallelukah, hal'li nafshi', for praising Hashem is 'na'im', pleasant.

The Beis Hamikdash is called 'heaven and earth' because it stood on earth yet, like heaven, was above place, time and number; so the help 'from Hashem, Maker of heaven and earth' can be the same kind of miracle for Jews now.
The miracle of space in Yerushalayim was not something one saw; it showed only when someone took a count of the people and the beds, while each person simply found a place to sleep.

A teacher who makes a pasuk or Midrash shine in his students' hearts has it quoted in his name, which is why the Ba'al haTanya brings a known Midrash in the Ba'al Shem Tov's name and why a pasuk in Mishlei appears in Avos in a Tanna's name.
The sign of the redeemer was not the words 'pakod pakadti', which everyone knew, but that when the true redeemer said them they would light up in the listeners' hearts.
Adar, the last month, is the darkest, yet because it is the end things suddenly turn over; for the same reason the Megillah shows no open miracles and no name of Hashem, since He is hidden.
'The sun will not strike you' means even success can harm, through envy and through a fall that comes from too much success; Hashem guards one who lives with hashgacha pratis from that.

Pharaoh's 'words of falsehood' were the Midrashim of redemption that the Jews read when they gathered on the Shabbos Moshe had won for them; by demanding the same output without straw he meant to make them work on Shabbos.

Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Rav distinguishes the one who trusts, the mivtach on whom he relies, and the thing he hopes for: the business is only a garment of hishtadlus, while Hashem must be the mivtach.
The extra yud of 'hayoshvi' is read as 'my' One who sits in heaven: each Jew has his own personal G-d who deals with him with individual attention.

Through the Radak, the Rav shows that a servant being struck looks to the very hand that strikes him, since no one else can save him from his master; so a Jew in suffering turns to the One who sends it.

The raised ayin of 'chazir miya'ar' is read as a hope that the ayin will become an aleph, turning the destructive forest boar of Rome into a harmless creature of the river, like the 'kosnos or' with an aleph that rectifies Adam's sin.
A repeated word in tefillah, which the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah would not add, is not part of the text but a reflexive cry from within, like a child's second 'quick!' or Eliyahu's second 'aneini'.
Turning the cheek to the striker is read as a way to end the blows: the striker is satisfied with the disgrace, and Klal Yisrael pleads that it has already had its fill of shame.

Since Jews did not merit that the nations come to them as in Shlomo's time, they must go out to the nations in galus, and the Chasam Sofer reads the plea to be gathered from the nations in this light.
The Rav reads 'if Hashem does not build the house' as David's prophecy about the churban of the very Beis HaMikdash his son would build, set in motion when Shlomo slept late before its inauguration.
Hiddurim belong to Torah and mitzvos; in business, which is only the fulfilment of Adam's curse, a person need not beautify his effort with extra hours.
Right after hinting at Shlomo's part in the churban, David calls him 'the heritage of Hashem', teaching that what was decreed in Hashem's plan is no blemish on Shlomo.
A newborn child is called a 'nachalah', a new territory from Hashem that opens a new channel of parnassah for the family.
Light-heartedly, the Rav reads 'ashpaso' as the household's refuse: the mud children track in is itself a blessing.

The same blessing of many children that a yerei Hashem treasures means nothing to someone of the 'mashkimei kum', so 'thus shall the man who fears Hashem be blessed' can only be said to a yerei Hashem.
Anger at another person is really anger at Hashem, since nothing good or bad can come through a person without Hashem's will; one who habitually thinks this way will never become angry.
From the Midrash's parable the Rav learns that relying on Hashem is itself the merit that saves: the king freed the man only because he had relied on him.
Chananiah, Mishael and Azariah were saved specifically in the merit of Yaakov, the one whose mention the wicked mocked, and the mockers were the ones burned.
Not fearing scoffers is the precondition for the whole Shulchan Aruch: one who fears mockery gains nothing from learning halachos he will not fulfill.
'Yoshev b'seser', which the Chashmonaim said going into battle, mentions no mitzvos, tefillos or merits at all, only bitachon itself.
Unlike Kiddush, where others fulfill their obligation through one person, on Chanukah the family itself lights, so when one member lights it is as though each has lit.
Because Chanukah is a mitzvah of the family, it increases each day, like a family that must grow.
Amalek's ability to stay unmoved by the splitting of the sea came from his view of everything as chance; this is the root of the war against him.
Calling the splitting of the sea a natural wind does not escape the miracle: that it came exactly when the Jews fled and the Egyptians pursued is itself a greater miracle.
Amalek's attack before Matan Torah brought a coolness into the Jews' acceptance of the Torah, which was completed only when Amalek was destroyed in the days of Purim.
Unlike religions built on one individual, the Torah rests on testimony that millions passed on to their children; a fabricated mass event would have been questioned by the very next generation.

Rates measured in a laboratory cannot be extrapolated back over eons, as water shows by expanding again near freezing; the Mabul's boiling waters could do in a short time what they reckon as a billion years.
Like electricity in a wire, which is unseen but known from what it does, Hashem's presence in the world is known from life and from the harmony of creation.

The Rav reads the difference between the two verses as two scenarios of the geulah: an early coming judged by the measure of Torah, and a delayed coming, after 'he comes, he comes' with nothing happening, judged by emunah alone.

Chavakuk's essence lies in his name, given with the words 'you will embrace a son': his message is embracing and holding on, and the emunah of 'a tzaddik lives by his emunah' is what the Jews hold on to through disappointments.

Darkness is not essentially dark: it is light too great to be received, as one is blinded by looking at the sun; this is why 'creating' is said of darkness, a higher level than 'forming' said of light.

The joy of Rabbi Shimon's day of passing comes from his power to reveal the hidden through the revealed; the Arizal taught no revealed Torah, so the joy hidden in the Nine Days of his passing is not yet fit to be revealed.
When learning has taste, that is the revelation of Rabbi Shimon; when it has none, one is like learning the Arizal's words, and one must still know that it is good.
The Rav reads 'I believe with complete faith' as also believing that one's own emunah is whole, even when questions trouble a person.

The Rav links Chizkiyahu's two puzzling acts: just as he held that a day merely fit to be Nissan is not yet Nissan, he held that being fit to be Moshiach is not yet being appointed, so he could not sing the tenth shirah.
There are souls of 'rishon' (Nissan) and souls of 'Adar', even of the second Adar pushed outside the order, and the redemption is delayed so that these too reach their tikkun.
The main victory came on the seventh of Nissan, the day of Efrayim's nasi, because Yosef, sold by the Yishmaelim, is holy bris milah, while Yishmael's milah is empty of content.
Chametz represents the nations, from whom some benefit can come, while se'or, unfit to eat, represents Yishmael, from whom no good comes at all.
A natural explanation of the splitting of the sea does not lessen the nes: the convergence of every factor at exactly that moment is an even greater, hidden nes, like Purim.
Shiloh's roof of curtains, and the lack of kedushah on the roof of the Beis HaMikdash, reflect that the roof corresponds to keser, and Amalek, 'ram' in gematria, blocks it until he is wiped out.
The present salvation is sweet and bitter: the comfort it brings in galus may mean the exile will last longer, as the Chasam Sofer's mashal of the banished prince shows.
The Purim miracles are not lesser for being hidden; they are greater, and precisely because they are so great they had to be concealed so that no harm could take hold of them.

Jewish dress works opposite to the nations' custom: they honor by uncovering, while Jews honor and guard holiness by adding layers, a yarmulke and over it a hat, because the Shechinah rests on the head of one who serves Hashem.
Achashverosh's 127 provinces express a lowered image of the heavenly order: seven for the lower world, twenty for the middle world and one hundred for the upper world, each placed in a lower 'digit'.

The sin at Achashverosh's feast was not the food but its spirit: attending a celebration that kingship remains with the nations is rejoicing in the exile of the Shechinah, even when everything served is kosher.
The dispute whether Achashverosh was wise or foolish is really a dispute about what reveals true kingship: the far who accept it, or the near who stand around the king.
In Heaven the feast that opens the Megillah is read as a feast for the distant: Hashem showed the Jews of the exile that the small service of a Jew in Adar outweighs the great avodah of Temple times.

Number and counting are a limitation of this world; the fiftieth day belongs to Heaven, so by Heaven's reckoning the day Moshe chose is the fiftieth even though the calendar calls it the fifty-first, and both days of Shavuos can be 'the time of the giving of our Torah'.

The place of the aron that took up no space, the pesukim of the Ten Commandments whose count does not fit, and the fiftieth day that is not counted all express one idea: where the Torah is, it is above time, place and number.
Emunah was received on the fiftieth day precisely because 'Anochi' was given above intellect; something understood is knowledge, and only something above understanding is believed.

The fiftieth gate of impurity is the mirror of the fiftieth gate of holiness: as holiness peaks in emunah, impurity peaks in apikorsus, and Amalek, whose gematria equals 'safek', puts doubt into Jewish hearts.
The suffering a bachur feels over his doubts is itself proof of his faith: someone who did not believe would be glad of the doubts.
A thought of doubt is sent from Heaven as an opportunity: the mitzvah of 'velo sasuru' is not that the thought never comes, but that one drives it out when it does.
'Chanina' is not only a person of the past but a type of soul present in every generation, the one who knows nothing is due to him, and for whose sake the world is still sustained.
The father's name 'Yochanan' is added to Matisyahu because, like Mordechai's lineage in the Gemara, it describes the same person's soul: a gift from Hashem, received as grace.

Rabbi Chanina could ask for vinegar to burn, although tzaddikim do not ask for miracles, because for him there was no difference between oil and vinegar; only one who thinks oil burns by itself sees a miracle in vinegar.
Bread growing from the earth is no less a wonder than manna falling from heaven; the generation of the desert was amazed by it only because they were used to the opposite.
Emunah is called 'Zeraim' because a Jew plants knowing the growth is a miracle; a gentile also plants and expects growth, but out of habit.
Zos Chanukah is the day the oil burned naturally, and that is its lesson: after seven days of miracles one recognizes that natural burning is also a miracle.
The order of the mitzvos parallels the order of the generations: they begin with Anochi and end with Chanukah, so the last generation is given the mitzvah of emunah.

Unlike every other nation, which falls when Hashem topples its heavenly prince, Amalek's prince is the yetzer hara in the Jewish heart; Hashem leaves this war to the Jews, and only when they win it does physical Amalek fall, the reverse of the usual order.

The two faces of Amalek, attacking milah and casting doubt in emunah, are one thing: the clear emunah of the Jews is Avraham's inheritance through the bris, so a blemish of the bris clouds the emunah.

Heresy comes from the heart, not the head: a person who will not admit a weakness invents a philosophy that justifies it, so the demand for logical proof is really a cover for a lack of shmiras habris.

Tefillin are the keser, worn on the body but not part of it, because Elokus lies beyond even the mind; they are black because emunah in galus has no grasp, and this is the 'yikar' written in the Targum-language of galus.
The orlah, an extra part on the body that belongs to no other creature, answers the heretic: if the body can hold something that does not belong to it, it can also carry tefillin, something above it.

Just as Mitzrayim is the 'ervas ha'aretz' of place, the era before Mashiach is the 'ervas hazman' of time, when heresy and immorality spread together; Purim, the last month of the year, is given as strength for it.

The emunah of today's Jews in the deepest darkness of galus gives Hashem a nachas ruach He did not have even in the time of the Beis HaMikdash, and in this the present generations are greater than earlier ones.
